deep.reconstruction:
Context: this page belongs to Riemann's student essay 'Versuch einer allgemeinen Auffassung der Integration und Differentiation' (dated 1847, published posthumously in the Gesammelte Werke, 1876). The essay defines a derivative of arbitrary (non-integer) order, written ∂_x^ν z, through a generalized Taylor expansion
  z(x+h) = Σ_ν c(ν) ∂_x^ν z · h^ν/Π(ν).
Here Π(ν) = Γ(ν+1), and the sum runs over ν in an arithmetic progression with step 1, unbounded in both directions. The coefficient function is c on the previous page; in the handwriting here it looks like l or k.

Previous page. Riemann shifts x twice, by h and then by k.
(α) z(x+h+k) = ΣΣ c(μ)c(ν) ∂^μ∂^ν z · h^μ k^ν/(Π(μ)Π(ν)). This covers all expansions of this form.
(β) z(x+h+k) = Σ c(μ+ν) ∂^{μ+ν} z · (h+k)^{μ+ν}/Π(μ+ν). Using the generalized binomial formula (3),
  (h+k)^s/Π(s) = Σ_ν h^{s-ν} k^ν/(Π(s-ν)Π(ν)),
this becomes ΣΣ c(μ+ν) ∂^{μ+ν} z · h^ν k^μ/(Π(ν)Π(μ)). Riemann notes that (β) need not give every expansion, because (3) supplies only one expansion of (h+k)^s/Π(s).

This page, step 1. All expansions contained in (β) must also be contained in (α). The transcription has 'x' here; the sense requires the formula label α.

Step 2. Comparing coefficients, impose the law
  l(μ+ν) = l(μ) l(ν)   (Cauchy's exponential functional equation).
Then every value of ∂^{μ+ν} z is also a value of ∂^μ ∂^ν z. The converse can fail, since the latter may have further values.

Step 3. Hence
  (5) ∂^μ ∂^ν z = ∂^{μ+ν} z
holds 'under the stated restriction', that is, as an inclusion of value sets for these many-valued objects. This is the index (semigroup) law for fractional derivatives.

Step 4, solving the functional equation.
- Induction gives l(μ+ν+π) = l(μ)l(ν)l(π). In general, the product of the l-values equals l of the sum.
- Setting all summands equal gives l(mν) = l(ν)^m for integer m.
- Put π = mν/n. Then l(nπ) = l(π)^n = l(mν) = l(ν)^m, so l((m/n)ν) = l(ν)^{m/n}.
- So l(μν) = l(ν)^μ for all rational μ. 'By the known law of interpolation' (in effect a continuity assumption) it holds for all μ.

Step 5, continued on the next page. Ordinary differentiation should be the special case, so l(ν) = 1 for integer ν. Therefore l(ν) = l(1)^ν = 1^ν. Read as many-valued, this is e^{2πikν}, which is 1 at integers.

Outcome: the generalized Taylor expansion becomes z(x+h) = Σ 1^ν h^ν/Π(ν) ∂^ν z.
errors: The passage from l(π)^n = l(ν)^m to l(π) = l(ν)^{m/n} only fixes l(π) up to an n-th root of unity. The ambiguity is not stated here; Riemann's later notation 1^ν (many-valued) implicitly absorbs it.

The extension from rational to real μ by 'the known law of interpolation' tacitly assumes continuity (or another regularity property) of l. Without it, Cauchy's equation has pathological solutions. This was standard practice in 1847, but it is an unjustified step by modern standards.

Law (5) is established only as an inclusion of value sets: every value of ∂^{μ+ν} z is a value of ∂^μ∂^ν z. It is not a genuine equality, as Riemann himself notes. The identity also depends on the unproved assumption that coefficients in such generalized power series expansions may be compared.
No mathematical slip in the algebra of the functional-equation argument.

results.what: Requiring the coefficient function of the generalized Taylor series to satisfy c(μ+ν) = c(μ)c(ν), so that fractional derivatives obey the index law ∂^μ∂^ν = ∂^{μ+ν} (as an inclusion)
results.modern_name: Semigroup / index law for fractional derivatives (Riemann–Liouville calculus)
results.usually_credited_to: Liouville (1832) for fractional calculus in general; this specific derivation via generalized Taylor series is Riemann's 1847 student essay, published 1876

results.what: Solving l(μ+ν) = l(μ)l(ν) through integers and rationals, then extending to all reals by continuity ('interpolation'), giving l(μ) = l(1)^μ
Conclusion l(ν) = 1^ν, so that ordinary differentiation is included as a special case
results.modern_name: Normalization of the generalized Taylor series z(x+h) = Σ h^ν/Γ(ν+1) D^ν z (the Riemann/Liouville form)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a manuscript page of Riemann's well-known student essay on fractional integration and differentiation, printed in his Gesammelte Werke (1876). The functional-equation argument is Cauchy's standard 1821 one. Nothing here is new or unattributed.

checkable.asserts: The exponential l(μ) = exp(aμ) satisfies l(μ+ν) = l(μ)l(ν); expected result 0.
The relation l((m/n)ν) = l(ν)^{m/n}, tested with specific integers m, n, k and real ν. It holds on the appropriate branch only, illustrating the root-of-unity ambiguity.
l(ν) = 1^ν = e^{2πikν} equals 1 at all integers ν, so ordinary derivatives are included.
Formula (3), the generalized binomial expansion (h+k)^s/Γ(s+1) = Σ_j h^{s-j}k^j/(Γ(s-j+1)Γ(j+1)), valid for |k| < |h|. Test numerically, e.g. s = 1/2, h = 1, k = 1/3.

transcription_corrections: 'auch in x enthalten sein' should read 'auch in α enthalten sein', referring to formula (α) on the previous page. The same α is probably meant in 'stellt man also für [α?] die Function l ...', but this is uncertain.
The coefficient letter rendered 'l' may be German-script 'k' (or correspond to c on the previous page); the reading is uncertain.
'gleich ist dem l ihrer Summen' should probably be 'ihrer Summe'.
'wenn man den einzelnen Factoren' should probably be 'die einzelnen Factoren'.
'der nun für ganze Werthe' should read 'da nun für ganze Werthe'.
The struck-out word '[feine?]' before 'also' is an unreadable deletion and should be ignored.
